Inspect lag and requeue failed delivery through the projector operations API. Built-in index helpers Looms includes built-in projectors for Memory, SQLite, and Postgres to keep a searchable run index and an approval index up to date: Helper Import When to use memory() @swirls/looms/projectors Unit tests and single-process development sqlite(opts) @swirls/looms/projectors/sqlite Local file path or existing db . Defaults to :memory: postgres(opts) @swirls/looms/projectors/postgres Production servers. Pass {'{ url }'} or an existing postgres.js client {`import { sqlite } from '@swirls/looms/projectors/sqlite' const index = sqlite({ path: './looms.db' }) // Query cross-run indexes from your admin routes: const run = await index.getActor(runId) const pendingReviews = await index.listReviews(runId)`} Custom webhook and fan-out projectors Any object implementing project(events) satisfies the Projector interface: {`import type { Projector } from '@swirls/looms/projectors' export function approvalsWebhook(url: string): Projector { return { name: 'approvals-webhook', version: '1', project: async (events) => { for (const event of events) { if (event.type !== 'approval.requested') continue await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ runId: event.runId, approvalId: event.payload.approvalId, title: event.payload.title, }), }) } }, } }`} Next: see complete working examples of custom projections in Examples , host runs on Durable Objects in Hosting & storage , or browse packages in Modules . ) }

title: Run, stop, resume
description: Build an agent that drafts a release announcement, then let a workflow wait for a human decision. Exit the process, start a new one, and approve or reject the same run. Its history and pending review survive.
text: Run, stop, resume Build an agent that drafts a release announcement, then let a workflow wait for a human decision. Exit the process, start a new one, and approve or reject the same run. Its history and pending review survive. This tutorial uses Bun 1.3 or later and local SQLite. It makes no network calls: the agent uses a deterministic turn function and publishing is simulated. The same definitions can use a real model and a production actor host. Create a project {`mkdir looms-starter cd looms-starter npm init -y npm install @swirls/looms zod`} The package installs from npm; Bun executes the TypeScript and provides SQLite. Pin @swirls/looms deliberately and commit your lockfile. Node alone cannot execute the Bun SQLite example. Define the work Save this as review-definition.ts . The workflow spawns a writer agent with a tool, asks for a decision, and checks the outcome before publishing. A rejection completes the workflow with published: false . Add durable storage Save this as durable-review.ts . SQLite holds the event log and snapshots; each invocation opens the same file. Run one command at a time—this is a single-process embed, not a multi-writer server. Start and stop {'bun durable-review.ts start'} The command prints a runId and exits. Copy that ID into the next commands. The pending approval is durable even when an aggregate run status still reads running ; inspect the approval projection to see what needs attention. {'bun durable-review.ts inspect YOUR_RUN_ID'} This is a new process. It should show one pending review and the agent/tool events recorded by the first process. Resume with a decision {'bun durable-review.ts approve YOUR_RUN_ID'} Expect status: "completed" and published: true in the output. Inspect it again: the result is still there, with no need to rerun the writer. Start another run and reject it instead: {'bun durable-review.ts reject ANOTHER_RUN_ID'} Expect published: false . A gate waits for a decision; it does not automatically treat rejection as an execution error. Always check the result before a consequential action. Make it yours Connect a real model and keep the review deterministic. Define a custom thread kind with its own state machine. Build a live React view of the same history. Deploy to Cloudflare Durable Objects with one actor per run. These source files are shared with the runnable examples and tested across separate processes. The full examples directory includes smaller patterns. ) }

title: Reliability and recovery
description: Durability depends on the host and storage you choose. In-memory examples lose history on exit. SQLite persists locally; production actor hosts must preserve one writer per run and provide wake scheduling.

sections.title: Replay and recovery are different operations
A crash after an external action

text: Reliability and recovery Durability depends on the host and storage you choose. In-memory examples lose history on exit. SQLite persists locally; production actor hosts must preserve one writer per run and provide wake scheduling. Replay and recovery are different operations Historical replay folds recorded events to reconstruct state and does not dispatch effects. Recovery loads a snapshot and later events, then resumes unfinished work. An effect that lacks a recorded outcome may execute again. Looms does not promise exactly-once actions across arbitrary external services. A crash after an external action Looms requests an external action. The service performs it. The host stops before recording success. Recovery cannot infer success from the local log alone. Pass ctx.effectId as an idempotency key where the external API supports it. Check that the service retains the key for as long as you may need to retry the action. For unsupported APIs, store a durable operation ID, query the provider for the outcome, or reconcile before retrying. Never assume adding an arbitrary header makes an API idempotent. Retries and errors Effect retry policies count total attempts: maxAttempts: 3 means one initial attempt and up to two retries. Attempt starts and retry deadlines are recorded before the runtime waits, so a restart preserves the retry budget and backoff. Configure start, heartbeat, and execution timeouts for work delivered to external workers. Worker callbacks include the effect ID and attempt number; stale callbacks cannot complete a newer attempt. Exhaustion records runtime.effect.failed . Signals and webhook delivery Use the embed start/signal idempotencyKey option with a stable runId for retries of the same logical request. Verify webhook signatures and transform allowed webhook payloads into typed events on the server. Deduplicate by the provider delivery ID and correlate by run, thread, and domain identifiers. Retrying with a fresh key defeats deduplication. Interrupted model streams A model call can produce partial deltas before failing. Those deltas may already be recorded; resuming work may incur another model call and different output. Render partial content as provisional, inspect completion events, and decide how your application handles abandoned partial turns. The adapter does not guarantee exactly-once billing or identical regenerated text. Snapshots, retention, and projections A compatible snapshot bounds replay work; it is not a backup or a schema migration. Trimming events removes older audit and time-travel history and can prevent rebuilding new projections from the beginning. Define a retention and archive policy before enabling trimAfterSnapshot. Projectors run after local commit. Durable delivery stores a cursor per projector name and version, retries without advancing that cursor, and dead-letters exhausted batches. A run can finish before an external index or webhook catches up, so monitor lag and keep projector writes idempotent. Test recovery Test a restart while parked, an interruption during an external action, duplicate webhook delivery, and a deployment with existing runs. The testing guide provides the local restart test. Review versioning before changing definitions. ) }

title: Authentication and tenancy
description: Looms hosts expose execution APIs. Your application supplies authentication, authorization, and tenant ownership. A runId is an identifier, not a secret or permission token.

sections.title: Do not expose unrestricted event ingestion
Keep secrets and private events server-side
Restrict access to the execution host

text: Authentication and tenancy Looms hosts expose execution APIs. Your application supplies authentication, authorization, and tenant ownership. A runId is an identifier, not a secret or permission token. Authorize requests before forwarding them Authenticate a session or service identity. Resolve the run's owner from your authoritative database. Authorize the requested operation: viewing history, sending a message, making a decision, or cancelling work. Validate and construct an allowed event on the server. Forward only the authorized request to Looms. Enforce this for reads and SSE subscriptions as well as writes. Every /runs/:id path exposes run data. For new runs, generate/assign ownership on the server; do not trust a tenant ID or arbitrary run ID from a browser. Do not expose unrestricted event ingestion A valid schema proves a payload's shape, not its authority. An untrusted client must not forge internal lifecycle events, payment outcomes, or another person's approval. Prefer purpose-specific application endpoints that accept a user intent and construct a narrow set of events. Keep secrets and private events server-side Model keys, credentials, and service modules stay on the host. Share only browser-safe catalogs and projections. A UI projection does not redact its input stream: if you send the full log to a browser, that browser can read every event in it. Filter or serve an authorized read model when events contain private information. Browser and webhook protections With cookie sessions, implement your framework's CSRF and origin protections for mutations. Configure CORS deliberately. Use TLS. Validate webhook signatures before parsing them as commands, cap request sizes, rate-limit starts and signals, and verify provider event IDs against a durable deduplication record. Approval authorization Authorize the actual approver and operation, not merely the existence of an approval ID. Handle concurrent decisions and late replies in the same server-side approval handler. Record who decided and which inputs they reviewed without placing secrets in events. Restrict access to the execution host The deployment guide disables the public workers.dev endpoint by default. Call the Worker through a private service binding or configure an authenticated gateway before enabling a public route. A service binding restricts access to the host but does not replace per-user authorization in your gateway. ) }

title: Test execution and recovery
description: Test the application's observable behavior: whether a rejected action occurs, whether a pending wait survives restart, and whether replay changes anything outside the runtime.
text: Test execution and recovery Test the application's observable behavior: whether a rejected action occurs, whether a pending wait survives restart, and whether replay changes anything outside the runtime. Use deterministic agents The quickstart's writer uses runTurn and a typed tool without a model API. This makes approval and recovery tests reproducible. Keep model quality evaluations separate from runtime correctness tests. Exercise both decision branches Start the release workflow, find its pending approval, and send approve or reject. Assert on the publication result, not just workflow completion. Rejection is a valid completed business outcome. Use the complete executable test below in the same directory as the two quickstart files. {'bun test durable-review.test.ts'} Each command runs in a different process against the same temporary SQLite file. The test verifies a pending review survives exit, either decision resumes it, and the final result survives another restart. Module and replay helpers Install @swirls/looms/testing for createTestRuntime, assertReplayDeterministic, and moduleConformance. createTestRuntime supplies an in-memory store and a run helper for Effect-based runtime operations. assertReplayDeterministic compares repeated folds of a log; it does not prove external idempotency or compatibility with future code. Before deploying Fault-inject an interrupted effect with a provider-supported idempotency key. Send duplicate and conflicting webhook/approval requests through your gateway. Load a snapshot and history produced by the previous application version. Test authorization for another tenant's run and event stream. Disconnect and reconnect the UI while execution continues. Verify your backup restoration and downstream index backfill. ) }

title: Troubleshooting
description: Start with the recorded events and the host logs. A UI that has stopped updating does not necessarily mean execution stopped.

sections.title: Reject still executes the next node
The agent produces a stub response
Timers do not fire after a local restart

text: Troubleshooting Start with the recorded events and the host logs. A UI that has stopped updating does not necessarily mean execution stopped. Unknown definition or kind Register the definition on its owning module. Register child definitions as well as roots. Install the module implementing the kind. Check exact names and retain old definitions for parked runs after deployments. A gate never resumes Read pendingApprovals, use the pending approvalId, and send a decision through your authorized gateway. Check correlation fields and event type. A gate has no automatic timeout. An approval.timed_out event alone does not resolve a wait for approval.decided. Reject still executes the next node A completed gate means a decision arrived. Check outcome === 'approve' before requesting the action. The quickstart publishes only after an explicit approval. Its restart test also checks rejection. The agent produces a stub response Supply {'agent({ llm })'} or a runTurn implementation. Omitting the adapter intentionally uses deterministic behavior. Check server-side environment variables and the provider model ID. SQLite fails under Node The @swirls/looms/core/bun-sqlite entry uses Bun's native SQLite module. Run this example with Bun, use the Cloudflare storage adapter in Workers, or implement another compatible store for a custom host. SSE does not update Confirm the request reaches /runs/:id/events with the correct permission context. Preserve text/event-stream and streaming bodies through the gateway, disable buffering, and check network errors. A disconnected client should resume with Last-Event-ID; ensure retention has not removed the requested history. Invalid input or events Compare the payload with the module's runtime schema. Use typed builders rather than handwritten envelopes. Compile-time payload markers do not add runtime validation. Inspect HTTP status and body; different hosts may map routing failures differently. Global run listing returns 501 This is the actor host contract. Use your application registry or a cross-run index; see the operations guide. Timers do not fire after a local restart Reopen the affected run cell to rescan timers. A stopped Bun process cannot fire in-process timers, and the local actor host does not enumerate persisted files for you. Use Durable Objects for host-managed alarms. Report a reproducible problem Include package versions, host/runtime version, a minimal definition, expected behavior, and sanitized event types/sequence. Remove credentials, prompts containing private data, and personal identifiers before opening a GitHub issue . ) }

title: Changing deployed code
description: A run records the exact version of every definition it starts. Recovery resolves that version, so the host must keep its implementation registered while the run can still wake. Looms does not store the historical code bundle for you.
text: Changing deployed code A run records the exact version of every definition it starts. Recovery resolves that version, so the host must keep its implementation registered while the run can still wake. Looms does not store the historical code bundle for you. This durability contract is separate from the SemVer version of @swirls/looms . A compatible package upgrade can still require a durable-definition or event migration for your application. Keep old definitions available Set the definition's version , and register old and new versions together. Starts and child spawns persist kind:name@version ; they never resolve to a floating latest version. Keep shared reducers and event contracts compatible with both versions. Evolve events additively Existing logs contain old payloads. Prefer optional fields with defined defaults or new event names for incompatible meanings. Keep old logs and snapshots as compatibility test fixtures. A module's protocolVersion is descriptive metadata, not an automatic migration engine. Plan snapshot changes Reducers and snapshot state must agree. Test loading existing snapshots before deployment. When a change is incompatible, keep the old implementation routed to old runs, migrate those runs with your own tools, or let them finish before retiring the old code. Do not rewrite historical events casually to make a new reducer accept them. A deployment procedure Inventory active and parked runs through your run index. Run old-history and snapshot compatibility tests. Deploy code that can still execute old definitions. Start a canary using the new definition and exercise reject, timeout, and restart paths. Monitor failures and keep the prior deployment available. Retire old definitions after their runs finish and you no longer need them for retained history. Rollback limits A rollback cannot undo external actions. Old code may not understand events written by a new deployment. Plan forward-compatible readers or a controlled recovery procedure before rollout. Restoring a database backup also requires reconciling actions performed since the backup. ) }

title: When to use Looms
description: Looms is a TypeScript execution runtime that you deploy in your own infrastructure. Use it when several kinds of work need to share durable state: an agent delegates to a workflow, a custom state machine waits for a webhook, and a human decides what happens next.

sections.title: One run, many kinds of work
When a simpler approach is enough

text: When to use Looms Looms is a TypeScript execution runtime that you deploy in your own infrastructure. Use it when several kinds of work need to share durable state: an agent delegates to a workflow, a custom state machine waits for a webhook, and a human decides what happens next. One run, many kinds of work A thread is a unit of execution with a kind and a state machine. Agents and DAG workflows are built-in kinds. Your own module can define a new kind using the same extension primitives. Threads nest within a run and share its ordered history, recovery, and projections. For example, a procurement agent starts a review workflow, which spawns a custom auction thread. The auction accepts bids until a deadline, records a winner, and returns a result to the workflow. The debugger can show the whole operation without joining logs from unrelated runtimes. Good fits Work that pauses for minutes or days on approvals, webhooks, or child results. Applications that combine model-driven decisions with deterministic business rules. Domain execution types that need more than a fixed agent loop or DAG. Products whose UI, audit history, and runtime state should come from the same events. Costs you take on You choose the host, enforce authorization, operate storage, and design compatible upgrades. Reducers must remain deterministic. External actions need idempotency or reconciliation. A single run has one writer. Put independent work in separate runs. When a simpler approach is enough A single model request, a stateless tool call, or a short request-response API may not need Looms. If your existing durable workflow engine already handles your execution model, adopting another one adds migration and operational work. Start with a specific need for custom thread composition or a shared execution history. How it fits existing tools Vercel AI SDK: keep its model providers. The Looms adapter calls the model while Looms schedules turns and tools. You do not run a second automatic tool loop alongside it. Durable Objects: supply the actor isolation, SQLite, and alarm host. Looms supplies thread composition, event history, effects, and projections. Temporal, Restate, DBOS, and other durable engines: Looms lets custom thread kinds share one run log. Compare the features and guarantees your application needs before switching. Your existing agent loop: adapt one turn through runTurn or a model adapter. Record the outcomes of external actions so execution can recover after an interruption. Release status and support Looms is an early 0.0.x library. Expect API evolution, pin the package version, and test recovery before production use. Cloudflare Durable Objects is the recommended production host; Bun with SQLite is the local path. Browser subpaths provide clients and projections. Custom hosts require you to preserve one writer per run. Try a complete run , then read integration and reliability . Source and issues: ByteSliceHQ/looms . ) }
